questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 3x3 Matrix
questions.problem:
A particular town has a fleet of $720$ bicycles for rent. The table below gives the pattern of rental and return locations over a typical day. 

|  |  | From: |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Museum** | **Station** | **Gym** |
| To: | **Museum** | $0.9$ | $0.3$ | $0.1$ |
| **Station** | $0$ | $0.3$ | $0.7$ |  |
| **Gym** | $0.1$ | $0.4$ | $0.2$ |  |

For example, $40%$ of the bicycles at the Station are moved to the Gym every day.

How many bicycles would eventually be located at the Station if the listed probabilities remained constant over many days?
questions.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.9 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.3 & 0.7 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & 0.2\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. 
As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.9 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.3 & 0.7 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & 0.2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 0 & -0.7 & 0.7 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & -0.8\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.3 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0 & -0.7 & 0.7 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & -0.8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 1 & 4 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & -7 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+3({x}_{3})+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=4{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}_{3}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 6{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, after many days, $\frac{1}{6}$ of the bicycles will be at the station. Therefore, the total number of bikes at the station after many days will be

$$
\frac{1}{6}\cdot 720=120.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Steady-State Vectors of Stochastic Matrices
questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.9 & 0.7\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}0.2 \\ 0.8\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the stochastic matrix $P$ and vector $q$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

- $q$ is a stochastic vector
- $Pq=q$
- $q$ is a steady-state vector of $P$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that $Pq=q.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $q$ is a stochastic vector since its entries are non-negative and add up to $1.$

- Statement II is false. Note that

$$
Pq=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.9 & 0.7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.2 \\ 0.8\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.02+0.24 \\ 0.18+0.56\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.26 \\ 0.74\end{aligned}]\ne q.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $Pq\ne q,$ it is not a steady-state vector of $P.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

choices.value: None of the statements are true

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 2x2 Matrix
questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0.9 \\ 0.5 & 0.1\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0.9 \\ 0.5 & 0.1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.5 & 0.9 \\ 0.5 & -0.9\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.5 & 0.9 & 0 \\ 0.5 & -0.9 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.5 & 0.9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-0.5{x}_{1}+0.9{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 5{x}_{1}-9{x}_{2} & =0 \\ {x}_{1} & =\frac{9}{5}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{5}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{5}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{14}{5}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{5}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{14} \\ \frac{5}{14}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a-b=\frac{9}{14}-\frac{5}{14}=\frac{2}{7}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 3x3 Matrix
questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.8 & 0.5 & 0.35 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.65\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above, what is the value of $a+b-c?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.8 & 0.5 & 0.35 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.65\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.9 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.8 & -0.5 & 0.35 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & -0.35\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.9 & 0.3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.8 & -0.5 & 0.35 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & -0.35 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 8 & -5 & 3.5 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & -3.5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3.5 & 0 \\ 8 & -5 & 3.5 & 0 \\ -9 & 3 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-8{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+9{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3.5 & 0 \\ 0 & -21 & 31.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 21 & -31.5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3.5 & 0 \\ 0 & -21 & 31.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{31.5}{21}{x}_{3}=\frac{3}{2}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}+2(\frac{3}{2}{x}_{3})-3.5{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{3}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}+\frac{3}{2}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 3{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 2x2 Matrix
questions.problem:
A town planning department wants to know how its citizens' preferences for traveling to work are changing. So they conducted a survey, and the results are shown below.

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Car** | **Subway** |
| To: | **Car** | $0.5$ | $0.6$ |
| **Subway** | $0.5$ | $0.4$ |  |

They found that $50%$ of those surveyed that currently drive to work are planning to switch to the subway next year, while $60%$ of the people surveyed that currently use the subway are planning to switch to their cars next year.

Assuming that the town has $50\,000$ that travel to work by car or subway, and the given probabilities remain constant over many years, how many people will eventually use their cars to drive to work? Round your answer to the nearest hundreds.
questions.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0.6 \\ 0.5 & 0.4\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0.6 \\ 0.5 & 0.4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.5 & 0.6 \\ 0.5 & -0.6\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.5 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0.5 & -0.6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.5 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{6}{5}{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{5}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{5}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{11}{5}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{5}{11}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{11} \\ \frac{5}{11}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, after many years, $\frac{6}{11}$ of the $50\,000$ people surveyed would use their cars. Therefore, the total number of people who will eventually use their cars is

$$
\frac{6}{11}\cdot 50\,000≈27\,300.
$$
